procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate taking cognizance of the offence and the consequent framing of the charge.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants moved the High Court by petition under s. 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for quashing the impugned order. The High Court dismissed the petition in limine (without going into the question). The Judgment and Order was dated 12.2.1986 of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Crl. Misc. Petn. No. 202-M/86.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave under s. 16(1) (a) (ii) of the Act. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and order passed by the High Court and that of the Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate, Moga.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Food (Health) Authority could sub-delegate his powers to institute prosecutions for an offence under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act to the Food Inspector.

facts: Under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, the Punjab State Government created Rule 3 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration (Punjab) Rules, 1958.
This Rule 3 allowed the State Government to delegate its power to authorize prosecutions to the Food (Health) Authority.
The State Government did so via a notification on October 10, 1968.
Subsequently, the Food (Health) Authority issued its own notification on September 7, 1972, attempting to further delegate (or sub-delegate) this power to the Food Inspector, Faridkot.
The Food Inspector then launched a prosecution based on the authority granted by the Food (Health) Authority.
law: Section 20(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, states that a prosecution can only be instituted by the Central or State Government, or by a person authorized by a general or special order from the Central or State Government.
Rule 3 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration (Punjab) Rules, 1958, allowed the State Government to delegate its powers, including the power to authorize prosecutions, to the Food (Health) Authority.
application: The Court determined that while the State Government could delegate its power to the Food (Health) Authority under Rule 3, this did not mean the Food (Health) Authority could then sub-delegate that power to someone else, like the Food Inspector.
The Court reasoned that Rule 3 must be read subject to the main provision of the Act, Section 20(1).

Section 20(1) only allows for authorization directly from the State or Central Government. It does not contemplate a scenario where an authorized person can then authorize another person (sub-delegation).
Therefore, the notification issued by the Food (Health) Authority on September 7, 1972, which purported to delegate his power to the Food Inspector, was beyond his legal authority (ultra vires).
The Court noted that the State Government could have directly authorized the Food Inspector, but it did not; the authorization came from the Food (Health) Authority, which was impermissible.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Food (Health) Authority could not legally sub-delegate his power to institute prosecutions to the Food Inspector. The notification attempting to do so was declared ultra vires (beyond his legal power) and void, meaning the Food Inspector was not competent to lodge the complaint.

issue.issue_text: Whether Rule 3 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration (Punjab) Rules, 1958, framed under s. 24(2)(e) of the Act, was ultra vires the State Government for being contrary to the legislative mandate in s. 20(1) of the Act.

facts: Under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, the Punjab Government created the Prevention of Food Adulteration (Punjab) Rules, 1958.
Rule 3 of these rules allowed the State Government to delegate its power to authorize prosecutions to the Food (Health) Authority.
The State Government delegated this power to the Food (Health) Authority.
The Food (Health) Authority then sub-delegated this power to a Food Inspector.
The Food Inspector filed a complaint against the appellants, who challenged the validity of this sub-delegation.
law: Section 20(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, states that prosecutions can only be instituted by the Central/State Government or by a person specifically authorized by them. This is considered an imperative safeguard.
Section 24(2)(e) of the Act gives the State Government a general power to make rules for the delegation of its powers and functions.
The legal principle that rules framed under a statute cannot contradict or go against the specific provisions of that statute.

The legal maxim 'delegatus non potest delegare' (a delegate cannot further delegate), which means a power delegated by a higher authority cannot be sub-delegated unless the statute explicitly allows it.
application: The Court determined that the power to authorize prosecutions under Section 20(1) is an important executive function, not a minor administrative one, and any delegation of this power must be construed restrictively.
It found that the Act, particularly Section 20(1) and the general delegation power in Section 24(2)(e), does not envisage or permit sub-delegation of the authority to launch prosecutions.
The Court reasoned that if Rule 3 were interpreted literally to allow the Food (Health) Authority to sub-delegate its power, it would contradict the specific mandate of Section 20(1) of the Act.

To resolve this conflict without striking down the rule entirely, the Court decided to "read down" Rule 3. It interpreted the rule not as a power to sub-delegate, but as the State Government's direct order authorizing the Food (Health) Authority itself to institute prosecutions.

Under this interpretation, the Food (Health) Authority was the person authorized by the State Government and had the power to prosecute, but did not have the power to delegate that authority further to the Food Inspector.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that Rule 3 of the Punjab Rules must be read subject to Section 20(1) of the Act and cannot be construed to authorize sub-delegation of the power to launch prosecutions. Therefore, the Food (Health) Authority's attempt to delegate its power to the Food Inspector was invalid. The Court effectively accepted that the rule, if interpreted to permit sub-delegation, was ultra vires the State Government for being contrary to the legislative mandate of the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Food (Health) Authority could sub-delegate his powers to institute prosecutions for an offence under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act to the Food Inspector.
appellant_arguments: By virtue of the authority derived under Rule 3, the Food (Health) Authority alone had the power to institute prosecutions for an offence under the Act and could not legally sub-delegate this power to the Food Inspector.
respondent_arguments: The Food (Health) Authority was competent to issue the notification to sub-delegate the power to prosecute, and therefore the complaint lodged by the Food Inspector was valid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Rule 3 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration (Punjab) Rules, 1958, framed under s. 24(2)(e) of the Act, was ultra vires the State Government for being contrary to the legislative mandate in s. 20(1) of the Act.
appellant_arguments: Rule 3 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration (Punjab) Rules, 1958, framed by the State Government in purported exercise of powers under s. 24(2) read with s. 20(1) of the Act, was ultra vires the State Government.
respondent_arguments: Rule 3 is in the nature of a general order in terms of s. 20(1) of the Act, and through it, the State Government validly delegated its powers to launch a prosecution to the Food (Health) Authority.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a statute, particularly one using negative language, prescribes that a power must be exercised in a specific manner by a designated authority, that requirement is absolute and mandatory. The power must be exercised only in the prescribed way, and any other mode of performance is forbidden. The authority to delegate a statutory power does not include the power to sub-delegate unless the statute expressly provides for it. Rules made under a statute cannot contradict or go beyond the provisions of the parent statute and cannot authorize a sub-delegation of power that the statute itself does not permit.
obiter: The maxim 'delegatus non potest delegare' (a delegate cannot delegate) indicates that sub-delegation of powers is not normally allowable, but the legislature can always provide for it.
Courts may be disposed to construe general powers of delegation restrictively when they concern important executive functions, as opposed to minor administrative functions.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A careful analysis of the language of s. 20(1) of the Act clearly shows that it inhibits institution of prosecutions for an offence under the Act except on fulfilment of one or the other of the two conditions. Either the prosecutions must be instituted by the Central Government or the State Government or a person authorised in that behalf by the Central Government or the State Government, or the prosecutions should be instituted with the written consent of any of the four specified categories of authorities or persons. The terms of s. 20(1) do not envisage further delegation of powers by the person authorised, except that such prosecution may be instituted with the written consent of the Central Government or the State Government or the person authorised.
legal_tests_applied: Where a power is given to do a certain thing in a certain way, the thing must be done in that way or not at all. Other modes of performance are necessarily forbidden.

The use of the negative words in s. 20(1) 'No prosecution for an offence under this Act ...... shall be instituted except by or with the written consent of' plainly make the requirements of the section imperative.

The use of the expression 'in this behalf' in s. 20(1) shows that the delegation of such power by the Central Government or the State Government by general or special order most be for a specific purpose, to authorise a designated person to institute such prosecutions on their behalf.
